## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.instead: Spell it "booking", and say plainly that all 7 had booking calls on their shift, which only shows the calls are there; whether any rang out unanswered is the next card.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 inside what you said · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip makes the 6 for, 1 against and the bar at 5 plain, but the axis reads '0 1 2 3 4 5 6 median 7', with the median label wedged between 6 and 7, so I have to look twice to see where people actually answered.
screens.why_b3: It is my frequency belief in my band of 5 to 7 days, but 'bokoing call' is a typo in both the belief and the question, and 'the most recent time it happened' makes no sense after a 7-day count, so it is recognisable but not cleanly my words.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' sends me on but does not say what near-daily booking calls on every shift mean for an AI that picks up the ones that ring out.
screens.why_b5: All 7 answered and were counted, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and it claims nothing beyond those seven.
screens.instead: Holding up: 6 of 7 agents had booking calls on 5 or more of their last 7 days (median 6), so the calls an AI could catch come in on almost every shift; a lean from 7 people, and the next card asks whether the unanswered ones matter.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 put it in their two against a bar of 5 of 7, so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The bars count 14 picks while the bar is 5 of 7 people, so I need a second look to square picks with people.
screens.why_b3: The title Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line usefully says unanswered calls are in the top two but not necessarily first, yet it does not tell me what to do with that for my pitch to hotel groups.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 is visible and called a lean, not a call, but the strip shows 6 for and 8 against as if it were people when 8 is picks from 7 people, which overstates the opposition.
screens.instead: Count the strip in people (6 for, 1 against, bar at 5) and add that the one against, Chiara, has a call center covering after hours, so groups like hers are where my pitch is weakest.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7", so I see that my belief held and the count that decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each answer is a bar with its count and for/against, the line marks where 'falls short' begins, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against out of 7 with my 5-of-7 marker, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The belief line is word for word what I checked, and the threshold 'A few rang out, all called back that day' is the one I set.
screens.why_b4: The So line spells out the gap: 4 of 7 lose most or all of the calls that ring out. It also tells me my answering solution is measured against that gap next, which is my pitch exactly.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, the screen says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the claim stops at 'these 7'.
screens.instead: Say the gap in my terms: for 4 of these 7, most calls that rang out were never called back, and that is the lost booking your AI answer has to win.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits beside "6 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7", and the line "Importance held, 6 of 7; the 1 who said no" ties the verdict to the count again before the quote.
screens.why_b3: The box is named Importance and carries my belief word for word: five hard things across a run of shifts, booking calls ringing out as one of the two I would most like made easier.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what the one dissent means for Codyco, for example whether groups whose call center already covers after six are a weaker segment or whether group emails are a second wedge, so I am left to work it out myself.
screens.why_b5: The n of 1 is plain and nothing is overstated, but the Current solution card had 1 of 7 against and this screen neither shows its why nor says where that person was asked, so the dissent looks like it was only on Importance.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's answer says a call center after six already covers the phones and the real drain is group requests and emails arriving without rates, which is something I did not type and which questions my own segment of groups that run a call center.
screens.instead: Add a Current solution box, or a note saying where its 1 against was asked, and close with a line like: 'Where a call center covers after hours, missed calls drop out of the top two and group emails take their place. Check whether your 5% holds for those groups, or aim at groups without after-hours cover.'

screens.why1: As the opening screen it checks whether I am the right person, so I see straight away why it is asked.
screens.why2: Central reservations office is our daily word, and it makes no difference to me whether they call it that or a call center, so I can answer at once.
screens.why3: I know which group I work for and that our Munich central office takes the booking calls.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it cleanly for a screener, and a screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: It says exactly the group and country it is aimed at, and nothing about a product comes through.
screens.why6: The question hears fine, but 'I'll read two options. Yes; or No.' is a stiff preamble for a plain yes-or-no, where the guidelines want just 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you work for a hotel group in Germany that has a central reservations office? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Asking a reservation agent whether a booking call came in on their shift is near-pointless, since we take dozens every shift, especially on a trade-fair Saturday, so the gate lets everyone through.
screens.why2: The question is plain apart from the typo 'bokoing', which makes me read it twice.
screens.why3: Booking calls on my shift are my whole working day, so I can answer this from what I do.
screens.why4: Yes and No are fine, but a gate should carry no escape, 'I'd rather not say' should not exist, and 'I can't recall one particular booking call' is a sentence that makes no sense when I take calls all day.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's point is calls that go unanswered, and asking only whether a call came in drifts away from that.
screens.why6: It is short and ends in 'Yes or no', but the interviewer would have to say the non-word 'bokoing' aloud.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call ring on your shift that nobody picked up? Yes or no.

screens.why1: It follows the yes on screen 2, but in a central reservations office booking calls come in all through every shift, so asking on how many days feels pointless when the real question is the calls we didn't get to.
screens.why2: 'Bokoing' is a typo I have to read twice, and 'on your shift' leaves me unsure whether to count the five days I worked or all seven days of the week.
screens.why3: I know exactly which days I worked last week, and booking calls came in on every one of them.
screens.why4: 1 to 7 covers it and 'I can't recall' fits, but the bare numbers don't separate days I worked from days in the week, so 5 for me means 'every shift' without saying so.
screens.why5: The founder's point is that not every booking call gets answered, and counting days with any booking call drifts away from that toward something every agent would answer 'all of them'.
screens.why6: It is short and 'say a number from 1 to 7' is easy to hold, but the voice will stumble on 'bokoing' and 'on your shift' is unclear when heard once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many of your shifts did a booking call ring out without anyone picking up? None · 1 or 2 · 3 or 4 · 5 or more · or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: After asking how often booking calls came in on my shifts, it makes sense to ask what part of the week I'd most want made easier.
screens.why2: "Your last run of shifts in a week" is clumsy, and wanting "booking calls that ring out unanswered" made easier reads oddly, since it's a problem, not a task, so I'd hear it twice.
screens.why3: I sit in the central reservations office in Munich, so the desk requests and the check-in and check-out rush are front-desk work I never see, and rates on every channel is mostly revenue's job, not mine.
screens.why4: My real answer is there, the calls we can't get to on a trade-fair Saturday, but two of five options belong to the front desk, and the call option isn't worded like the others, so it stands out.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's point about unanswered calls, but that option is the only one phrased as the problem itself, which tips me off to what the study is after.
screens.why6: One short question, five short options I can hold when read out, and a single escape said last.
screens.instead: Think of your shifts last week. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Getting to every booking call at peak times; Covering calls after hours and on holidays; Answering booking emails and group requests; Checking availability and rates while on a call; or Entering and changing bookings in the system. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After asking what I'd most like made easier, it makes sense to ask how the calls actually went on my side.
screens.why2: It tells me to think of one call and then asks how 'answering booking calls through a central reservations office or call center' went; that is a whole shift's worth, and nobody in our office talks about our own Zentrale that way.
screens.why3: I can say how my shift went and I see the queue board, but one last call can't tell me how many rang out, so I'd answer for the shift and partly guess.
screens.why4: The five steps from all answered to simply lost cover our Saturdays well, but they describe a run of calls rather than one call, and 'Someone else did it' hardly fits an agent who takes the calls herself.
screens.why5: The segment's wording 'central reservations office or call center' has been pasted into the stem, so it reads like the study's label for me, not a question about my phone.
screens.why6: The five options are held in one go, but the stem is long and the 'or call center' clause is a mouthful after an anchor about one call it doesn't follow.
screens.instead: Think of your last busy shift on the phones. How did the booking calls go? Every call answered or called back in minutes; a few rang out, all called back that day; some rang out, called back when there was time; many rang out, few were called back; or calls that rang out were simply lost. Or say I can't recall.
